Mirra.what: Follow X accounts from Telegram: every post arrives in minutes, and a short brief tells you what each author has been saying and how it changed.
Mirra.arch:
One paid fetch per author per cycle, shared by every subscriber tracking that handle; each subscriber re-applies its own content filter and time window locally. Fetching is priced per author — fan-out is free.

Upstream returns wrong authors, out-of-window posts, and second-precision timestamps. Four validation layers, in sequence:

LayerCatches
Client-side author validationposts attributed to the wrong account
Timestamp check, clock-skew tolerantout-of-window posts
30-day seen-setrepeats and re-serves
Snowflake-id tiebreakersame-second ordering collisions
  • Frozen packs. Documents are numbered and frozen before the model call, then shuffled — view-sorted packs concentrate the low-engagement tail mid-context, where attention is weakest. Shuffling flattens that bias.
  • One model call per author per window. Clustering, importance scoring, shortlist selection and citation verification run as deterministic code around the call. Tokens are spent on the writing only.
  • Continuity from prior output. Each brief is grounded on the previous brief's text, never re-fetched posts. A recurrence claim is downgraded unless its cited evidence appears verbatim in the current window.
Mirra.proc:
• The live prompt is a versioned database row, not code. A change ships as a new version and is measured against the one it replaces.
  • Retry logic was branched on evidence. Half of all parse failures sat exactly at the output-token cap, where a plain re-roll would have been inert.
  • A lint canary injects a violation on every commit. The build fails if the rule doesn't catch it — a dead rule and a clean tree exit identically, and this is the only way to tell them apart.
  • Copy is banked before it ships. Staging and production are separate deploy paths released on the operator's call, with user-facing copy approved in advance.

within minutes"] DD -->|"frozen pack, then one model

Mirra.imageCaption: Every post an author publishes is captured continuously; each cycle the window is frozen into a single document pack and written into one brief.
Mirra.hiCaption: One fetch per author fans out to every subscriber tracking them, and the brief written from that same capture is read by all of them.
glance: Posts land in Telegram within 5 minutes — sub-60s on Premium
One per author each cycle: topics, proportions, what shifted
~90% gross margin — one fetch and one brief serve every subscriber
Mirra.archHi:
Mirra turns X accounts into a Telegram feed. Everything downstream follows from one decision: work happens per author, never per reader.

  1. Watch. A collector claims each author. However many people follow them, upstream is asked once per cycle, and every subscriber shares that answer through their own filters and time window.
  2. Mirror. Posts land in your Telegram inside a minute, cleaned and in order.
  3. Brief. On your schedule, one AI pass condenses the window into a short brief: what each author said, and what changed since last time.

Every step is priced by authors watched, not readers served — a brief is written once and read by everyone. That's why costs stay flat as the audience grows.

Social Hook.what: It watches your development work and turns it into social posts in your voice — approved by you, or fully autonomous.
Social Hook.arch:
The commit hook backgrounds itself, so a commit is never blocked; unregistered repositories, off-branch commits and CI environments exit before any model call is made.

  • One adapter contract, applied four times. Publishing platforms, media generators, messaging channels and model providers all implement the same abstract shape — adding a platform is one factory function and one registration, never a new branch in a dispatch chain.
  • Capability flags, not platform names. Callers branch on what a platform declares it can do; one without threads or native quoting degrades to a link instead of failing.
  • Five model providers behind one normalised response type. The Claude CLI provider embeds its JSON schema in the system prompt rather than using structured-output mode — the cost is a multi-turn validation loop of three or more round trips.

Between an approved draft and a live post stand four gates, each holding the draft editable rather than failing it:

GateHolds when
Adapterthe platform has no adapter registered
Credentialsthe account isn't connected
Formatthe draft's format can't be auto-posted
Mediareferenced media hasn't resolved yet
Social Hook.proc:
• A wiring check treats a capability with no caller as unbuilt. The first live run found 112 functions that were complete, unit-tested and reachable from nothing — reviews are scoped to diffs, and a diff cannot show an absent caller.
  • Allowlisting requires a written reason. A blank reason fails the build, and bulk allowlisting isn't permitted.
  • Releases are cut automatically from conventional commits. CLI documentation is regenerated in CI and fails the build if it differs from what's committed.
  • Test counts are quoted per member, never as totals. Concurrent agents share one database, so a count only means something measured from a clean checkout inside a quiescence window.
Social Hook.mermaid:

in the background"] -.->|"trivial or CI"| STOP(("no post")) V["Voice references: identity, voice file,
rejections, prior posts"] --> CP["Composer"] C --> CP CP -->|"writes its own media spec"| G{"Four gates on the draft"} G -->|"held"| H["Back to draft,
still editable"] G -->|"clear"| PUB["Approved in Telegram, web or CLI,

Social Hook.hiCaption: Commits are classified and drafted, then held at a gate until approved, and only then published to each channel.
glance: Your actual commits and dev activity
Approval gates in Telegram, web or CLI — or hands-off
Open source on PyPI; B2B SaaS layer in design
Social Hook.archHi:
Social Hook watches your development work and turns it into posts in your voice. The pipeline runs from commit to published post:

  1. Notice. A hook watches your commits in the background and picks out the ones worth talking about.
  2. Draft. An AI composer writes the post in your voice, attaching media when it helps.
  3. Gate. Nothing publishes until it clears your approval — unless you've gone fully autonomous.
  4. Post. Live on X and LinkedIn today, with the platform list built to grow.

Your workflow never pauses for any of it: the hook returns before the commit finishes, and drafts wait for you rather than the other way round.

Clauded.what: Claude Code running inside a Docker sandbox: skip permission prompts safely while clipboard, sound, Chrome, git and MCP still reach your Mac.
Clauded.arch:
• Bridges are ordinary local HTTP services on the Mac. Container-side shims replace pbcopy, pbpaste, xdg-open and the sound player with clients that detect the container — run natively, they fall back to the real binary.
  • The microphone runs the other way. The host streams 16 kHz raw PCM into a container FIFO exposed as an audio source, and the socket is open only while that source is actually recording — the Mac microphone is live during capture, not for the whole session.
  • Consent is anchored host-side. A native dialog defaulting to Deny, a timeout that resolves to denied, a per-session cache, and a cooldown so a retrying client can't produce a prompt loop.
  • No secrets in the box. Every bridge request carries a token compared in constant time, and the container never holds an API key — authentication is the normal browser login, with credentials living in a mounted host directory.
  • Opt-in firewall. Egress drops by default; re-admitted are only the model API, the code host, two package registries and telemetry.
Clauded.proc:
• The changelog is append-only and never renumbered. An entry number stays a stable reference forever; each entry states symptom, root cause and fix.
  • A working bridge was deleted when its premise proved false. Claude in Chrome pairs over a cloud relay rather than localhost — the Mac-side proxy had never been necessary.
  • The build stopped pruning Docker images system-wide after it was caught deleting other projects' images — and the deliberate non-use is recorded in a comment so it isn't reintroduced.
  • The Linux port is published as an assessment, not started. Three hard blockers and four degraded features are named, and the already-portable parts are listed so they're never re-audited.
Clauded.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Container
    participant H as Mac bridge
    participant U as Operator

    C->>H: pbcopy, xdg-open, sound
    Note over C,H: token-checked local HTTP
    H-->>U: clipboard, URL, audio
    U->>C: starts voice capture
    C->>H: connects only while recording
    H->>U: dialog, defaults to Deny
    U-->>H: approved, cached 1h
    H-->>C: 16 kHz PCM, 100 ms chunks
    Note over C,H: nothing written to disk
Clauded.imageCaption: Five host bridges pass through an otherwise sealed container wall: clipboard, sound, URL opening, microphone, and mounted git and SSH credentials.
Clauded.hiCaption: The container is a hard boundary; five bridges cross it to reach the host.
glance: A hard container wall instead of soft permission prompts
5 host bridges: clipboard · sound · Chrome · git/SSH · MCP
As many in parallel as you want; resume by name
Clauded.archHi:
Clauded runs Claude Code inside a sealed Docker container, so it can work without permission prompts — and without being loose on your Mac. The container holds no keys and has no reach of its own; five bridges hand back the conveniences one at a time: clipboard, sound, Chrome, git and MCP.

Anything sensitive still asks the Mac itself. Consent dialogs are native, default to Deny, and time out as denied. And because a session is just a container, you can run as many in parallel as you like.

LikeWiki.what: Your X likes, compiled into a private wiki: every claim cites the post it came from, and the pages rebuild themselves nightly.
LikeWiki.arch:
Two page classes with opposite lifecycles carry the whole design:

Page typeLifecycleMay cite
Sourceappend-mostly, read-only to every agentnothing
Conceptrewritten nightly as material landssources only
  • Sources are read-only for a reason. A source body holds the full transcript and media descriptions and routinely exceeds a model's read cap — a rewrite from a capped read would silently truncate it.
  • Concept pages never cite each other. Sources are stable; concept pages are not. Citing only sources keeps every reference valid across nightly rewrites.
  • No database. Flat markdown in git is the store, and the reading surface never touches the working tree — each request pins one commit and reads every page from that revision, so an ingest run landing mid-request cannot produce a torn read.
  • Judgement is the model's only job. Tags, source counts and index ordering are computed by inverting the citation map — a tag is, by construction, a page that really does cite the source.
  • A read-only server for other agents. Catalogue, page summaries, source search and raw sources, every response stamped with its commit and age so a stale checkout announces itself.
LikeWiki.proc:
• Video ingest verifies magic bytes after download. A field-name mismatch had been saving thumbnails under video filenames, so a single still was described as if it covered a two-hour talk — 40 source pages were invalidated before the mismatch was spotted.
  • The fix was re-landed with a measurement after a refactor silently reverted it: 57 of 58 affected videos were recoverable from URLs already stored.
  • Audits are owed by content fingerprint, not commit history. A page audited in one month and extended the next is owed another — the previous heuristic counted it as done.
  • Self-reports weren't trusted. Rewriting agents reported their own work clean; 24 independent adversarial auditors then found six real defects, including an attribution to the wrong speaker entirely.

transcribe media"] SC --> CT["Categorise
one source, full ripple"] CT --> G[("Flat markdown
in git")] subgraph SUP["Supervisor tier"] direction LR B["Backfill"] --> E["Entity pass"] --> A["Grounding audit
by fingerprint"] end G --> SUP SUP --> G G -->|"reads pinned
to one commit"| R["Reader and
agent server"]
LikeWiki.imageCaption: Concept pages are held together by their citations: each claim is threaded back to the source post that states it, and the pages are what the threads gather into.
LikeWiki.hiCaption: Liked posts converge into concept pages, and every claim on a page threads back to the source that states it.
LikeWiki.archHi:
LikeWiki compiles the posts you like on X into a private wiki. The unit of trust is the citation: every claim on every page traces back to the post it came from.

  1. Collect. Liked posts arrive with their media and are kept in full as source pages.
  2. Read. Each source is read in its entirety, categorised, and woven into the concept pages it belongs to.
  3. Rebuild. A nightly pass rewrites, audits and repairs the whole wiki as new material lands.

Pages change nightly; sources never do. Whatever a page says today, the post behind it is one click away.

Track Record.what: Public predictions, kept honest: every call goes into a ledger, gets tracked to its outcome, and scores the person who made it.
Track Record.arch:
Capture is one additional model call over a document pack that already exists, against a versioned prompt — no new pipeline. The ledger is a typed scoring contract over an open payload: everything the model returns is stored losslessly, and only the fields a resolver or a filter computes on are typed.

Resolution is partitioned by three clocks:

ClockSettles
Market dataany claim carrying a resolvable spec
The author's own later poststhe ~60% of calls with no time signal at all
Policy capsonly what never had a horizon
  • Subjects are canonical at creation, never free text. Tickers for equities, series identifiers for macro, coin identifiers for crypto, knowledge-base identifiers for people and policies — and an author-local subject when nothing matches, so capture never blocks.
  • Claims are immutable. A restatement annotates; a revision opens a new linked segment. An author can never walk back an entry, and price anchors are captured once at insert, never recomputed.
Track Record.proc:
• Only facts are stored. Verdicts, including the score, are render-layer and versioned — the formula can change without rewriting history.
  • Resolution rate is instrumentation, never scoreboard. What counts as checkable is partly the classifier's judgement on marginal cases, so a public percentage would move whenever the extractor is revised.
  • The classification vocabulary is itself a versioned row. Every labelled example stamps the version it was labelled under; a change ships as a new version with notes, never as an edit.
  • A call that reaches its horizon unresolved is graded against the relevant index. Never scored as a miss, never dropped — dropping it is the cherry-pick the product exists to expose.
Track Record.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Extracted
    Extracted --> NotACall: opinion
    Extracted --> Stance: thesis
    Extracted --> Open: a grounded call

    Open --> Hit: target touched
    Open --> Miss: stop touched
    Open --> Void: never triggered
    Open --> Reversed: author u-turns
    Open --> Graded: horizon, tape exists
    Open --> Stale: horizon, no tape
    Open --> Review: readers disagree

    Review --> Open: operator adjudicates
    Stance --> Stance: restated or reversed
Track Record.hiCaption: A public claim enters the ledger, is driven to a terminal state, and becomes a score shown beside the partition it came from.
glance: Live sentiment and who backs or disputes whom
Track Record.archHi:
Track Record keeps public predictions honest. Every call becomes a structured claim in a ledger, and every claim is carried to an ending — hit, miss, or void.

  1. Capture. Predictions are pulled from what a person actually published and stored as claims against canonical subjects — a ticker, a coin, a named series — so the same subject is the same subject everywhere.
  2. Resolve. Each claim is tracked until reality settles it.
  3. Score. Authors are scored on their whole history, never the highlight reel.

Sentiment and who-backs-whom sit alongside the scores, adding context to every call.

Claude Historian.what: Makes past Claude Code sessions searchable — what was tried, what worked, what was decided. My contribution took search from 45% to 100% of history.
Claude Historian.arch:
• No index, no database, no background process. Transcripts stream from disk per query, behind a file-level pre-filter that runs before anything is parsed as JSON.
  • The read strategy was benchmarked, not assumed. Files under 400 KB are read whole and split; larger ones stream line by line. The crossover point came from measurement.
  • Two-stage ranking. A per-message term score, then a multiplicative refinement with capped match boosting — it replaced an inverse-document-frequency computation the corpus was too small to justify.
  • The coverage fix. Project directories are walked recursively and subagent hits roll up to their parent session with per-agent counts. One-result-per-subagent was rejected after a single session turned out to have spawned 1,239 of them.
  • Discovery needed a resolver first. Subagent directories are named after their parent session, so recursive discovery without a real session resolver would answer “summarise this session” with one subagent's transcript instead.
Claude Historian.proc:
• An evaluation harness came before any change. The repository had no behavioural tests, so one was built first — each fixture asserts one direction only and is pinned at session level, so a later change in result shape cannot break the assertion.
  • Phases were ordered by dependency, not value. Recursive discovery more than doubles the bytes scanned, so it couldn't land until the scan got cheaper — a raw-byte, case-insensitive pre-filter measured 3.7× faster than a lowercased-copy scan on identical results.
  • A full-text sidecar index was designed, then cancelled. Session-scoped search alone took the reported complaint from 6,500 ms to 4 ms; the sidecar bought latency only on global search, at the cost of a plaintext copy of every conversation.
  • One negative result stayed in the record. A hand-written character-code fold ran about 50% slower than native lowercasing on line matching — raw bytes win only where they avoid a decode.

Claude Historian.archHi:
Claude Historian makes past Claude Code sessions searchable — what was tried, what worked, what was decided. There is nothing to install or keep in sync: no index, no database. Search scans the transcripts on demand and returns compact summaries sized for an AI's context window.

My contribution fixed its blind spot. Work delegated to subagents lived in directories the search never visited, so it saw 45% of history; the fix made all of it searchable, rolled up under the sessions that spawned it.

Xactions.what: A full X operations suite an AI agent can drive — publishing, analytics, audience CRM, monitoring and autonomous personas, through one MCP surface.
Xactions.arch:
• Three data paths behind one surface. A stealth-configured browser, direct calls to the platform's own internal endpoints, and nine interchangeable engine adapters.
  • A session cookie, not a developer key. The tool surface is as wide as the account holder's own reach, not as narrow as an API tier.
  • A persona is a long-lived loop, not a cron job. An activity pattern decides whether it should be awake at all; a strategy sets daily ceilings on follows, likes, comments and posts; each session's budget is jittered so activity never lands on a machine-readable rhythm.
  • Streams are durable polling. Repeatable queue jobs against a pooled browser, a per-stream lock against overlapping polls, exponential backoff on consecutive failures.
  • Bulk clears four gates before anything executes. A blacklist, per-action daily caps, a hard refusal above a hundred actions without an explicit override, and a resumable progress file.
Xactions.proc:
• Testability drove one refactor. The article extractor's boundary-stripping was lifted out of the browser closure into a plain module — a closure that exists only inside a page evaluation cannot be referenced from a test.
  • Silent failures ship with their diagnosis. Query identifiers for internal endpoints rotate upstream and fail by returning nothing while everything visible still works, so the fix records how to recognise the next rotation, not just the new value.
  • Working-tree-only tools were committed. A clean reinstall would have removed a dependency another project was built on.

Xactions.archHi:
Xactions gives an AI agent full command of an X account through one MCP surface: publishing, analytics, audience CRM, monitoring and Spaces, every operation a typed tool the agent can call.

Personas can run an account autonomously on a schedule, inside daily ceilings. Bulk actions stay behind explicit approval and hard caps.

Stellar Explorer.what: An explorable 3D map of the night sky: fly between 117k stars, open any into a detail view, with sound tied to the journey.
Stellar Explorer.arch:
• One shader program serves every body. Three procedural surface functions blended by step masks on a type uniform — no branch in the fragment path, no second program to compile.
  • Moons are created on expand and released on collapse. Geometry, materials and children are walked and disposed, not hidden.
  • Five-pass composite. A tone-mapped render at a capped pixel ratio, then bloom, vignette, chromatic aberration and film grain — the last three written by hand.
  • The background is procedural too. Three counter-rotating point shells with additive nebula sprites drawn to canvas at runtime; depth and parallax cost no texture assets and no network fetch.
  • Hover raycasting at 20 Hz. Hits route by user-data tags, so a single cast distinguishes a click on a body from a click on the void that body becomes.
Stellar Explorer.proc:
• Interaction feel was tuned before features were added. Orbits freeze on hover and in detail view, and the camera offsets its target so a body sits off-centre with room for the reading panel.
  • Audio is synthesised, not loaded. The one audible cue is the one whose gain envelope peaks together with its noise buffer — the others are inaudible by measurement, not missing by omission.
Stellar Explorer.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Orbiting Orbiting --> Focused: click a body Focused --> Expanded: void and disk appear Expanded --> Expanded: a moon does the same Expanded --> Collapsing: click the void Collapsing --> Orbiting: children spiral in,
everything disposed note right of Expanded moons are built on first expand, never before end note
Stellar Explorer.imageCaption: A body sits in a procedural field of three counter-rotating point shells and additive nebula sprites, all generated at runtime with no texture assets.
Stellar Explorer.hiCaption: Every body opens into its moons, and each moon opens the same way.

Stellar Explorer.archHi:
Stellar Explorer is the night sky as one explorable 3D scene: 117,000 stars, and any body opens into its own detail view when you reach it. Moons don't exist until the first time you visit their planet — each world builds itself on arrival and is torn down when you leave.

Sound follows the journey.
